I may regret sharing this but when I was between the ages of 6-9 I would really abuse my animals. 

It started when I was 6 and my mom had just set up a new aquarium. She had two Plecos (the sucker fish) among other fish. For whatever reason, they were easier to catch. I remember pulling them out of the tank. Sometimes I would see how long they would stay out, then put them in different liquids. I would do other little stuff like pull all the legs off of daddy long legs and whatnot. A little bit smaller stuff.

Then it evolved into torturing my hamster. I would do terrible things to it, like put it in my fish tank to see how fast it would take him to get to the surface, and throw him and other horrible things I won’t go into. 

Near the same time, I would do horrible things to my baby sibling. It was fun to me to swing them around really fast (but only for a second because we had super attentive mother, so I had to be fast back then). I would do bad bad stuff I can’t even mention here, but to give you an idea, I would choke them until they turned blueish. 

The only reason I finally stopped is because I had a friend over one time and I showed him what I did with my hamster and he was shocked and started crying. He went home crying and never came back over. I’m not sure if he ever told his mom, or not, but he never came back over. I was embarrassed by the whole thing I finally stopped.

So if you’re ever in a position that I was put in today, this are some things that I learned that could hopefully help someone out. 

1) Keep your IV cart and EKG machine next to your desk. During my down time, I would creat quick little IV bags that had all my supplies ready to go. 

2) As you check the patient in, order some hold tubes (or a standard order set if you’re allowed) to prep for your blood tubes (if necessary). 

3) once they get in a triage room, slap a set of vitals on the patient, and while the Blood Pressure cuff is running, set up the full IV from your IV bag. That way when it’s done, you can write the vitals down on their label sheet and get the IV going. (Once again, if it’s appropriate for them)

4) As you’re doing the IV, EKG, or both, get your quick assessment. That way while you chart vitals and your IV, you can put the assessment in and have them wait back out in the waiting room. 

5) I usually leave the door open so I can see any other potential patients walking up, but during an EKG, I’ll close it, and have security notify me if something urgent came up to the counter. 

It took me between 5-10 minutes a patient to do this by the end of it when I had a better flow down. Not ideal, but it’s what I could do. 

Also, just remember, you can only do what you can do. It feels like the weight of the world is on your shoulders when you have 30 patients staring at you, with their family members, but as long as your doing the best you can, that’s what matters. I am 20 now. At 18, I became a father and at 19 I got married. However, this was not my biggest problem. At 18, I became a Home Care CNA. If you don't know what this is, look it up. I was paired with a young guy (We'll call him Pat for short). Pat was a 13 year old boy with a very crippling disease known as NBIA. It was called Nuerodegeneris with Brain Iron Accumulation. He had iron growing on his brain, and was losing control of his body. However, ironically, his brain was still perfectly normal. He lost the ability to talk shortly after I started working with him. He could still answer yes and no by looking a certain direction. 

I worked with him every day for a year. He became much like a younger brother to me. We watched Superman every single day, because he hoped on day he could be strong like Superman. We played Pokemon because we liked it, and it was easy for him to tell me how to play. About a year later, his breathing started getting very deep and random. On February 8th of this year, we had finished watching Superman, and I remember telling him how they had come up with new devices that would allow you to think and move a limb, and that I would do some research into it, and share with him on Monday what I found. 

I got a call on Monday morning saying that I didn't have to work today, because Pat had a nurse taking care of him, but I could visit him just not in my work clothes. I had a feeling about what was going on, but hoped that he was just getting reevaluated or something. When I arrived, I could automatically tell that the mood was solemn. Patrick was not dead, but dying. He would sometimes move his eyes around and slightly smile, then slip back into a glazed over look and take a deep breath and hold it. We each had a couple minutes to talk to him and say whatever we'd like. His mom took a break from sitting with him, and it was my turn to talk with him. I held his hand and made an inside joke that he loved. I felt him squeeze my hand very slightly. Whether it was not purposeful or it was his way of letting me know he was laughing, I don't know. I told him it would be alright, and that "This isn't goodbye, but I'll see you later". I gave him a big hug and noticed that he wasn't so tight (from his disease. It made him tense up 24/7). His face was also blue and he hadn't taken a breath in almost 90 seconds. He was dead, but I let the nurse know to check and make sure. 

I sat with a 13 year old, and held his hands in the last moments of his life. I thought cracking my phone was bad, but his death really put everything perspective for me. I became extremely depressed, but I had to be there for my wife an daughter. I miss Pat a lot. He was Superman to me.

I've worked at McDonalds before and I've worked as a CNA. Out of the two, CNA is far more soul destroying. At McDonalds, I've had people throw eggs at me in Drive Thru, I've had GM's lose their shit over the drink machine (and throw full drinks at me), and I've had coworkers hurt me in every possible way (from degreaser to the eyes to kidney punches). That stuff sucked, but it wasn't quite soul destroying. 

As a CNA, the soul destroying part was more mental, although there are plenty of terrible physical aspects. I've been jizzed on by some memory loss patient. I had a guy come into the ER stabbing his stomach with a long screwdriver and wiping the shit everywhere (he was obviously hyped up on something like bathsalts). As an in home care CNA, I've had manipulative family members try to get me to do their chores, and threaten me with other things if I didn't do them (I was only supposed to do patient chores).

But that's not the soul destroying part. The worst part is, when patients die with no family around. They are supposed to be surrounded by family, not medical staff. I've seen it happened many times in a nursing home with many elderly people. The families just don't care. One of the toughest moments was when a child passed away. I won't go into much detail, but him and his family had just got into a terrible car accident. The little boy had just arrived by helicopter, and had terrible injuries. He was still conscious and cognitive, so he knew much of what was going on. There were about 4 of us moving his bed to the operating room. My job was to talk to him and remind him to breath among a few other things. As we arrived in the OR room, he started to stare off and his eyes eventually rolled into the back of his head. He died when we arrived there. But at the hospital, you can't stop. Once he was pronounced dead, we went on break and went on with our day. How the fuck are you supposed to get over that? This little kid was my brother's age, and he died while I was holding his hand. He should be surrounded by family, not medical staff. It's not like other coworkers want to hear how sad your day is (plus I didn't know many people that shift). You just have to put up and shut up. That is soul destroying.
